A Moral Reckoning: The Case for a One-Time Wealth Confiscation

[Address delivered to the gathered assembly]

My friends, my neighbors, my fellow citizens of this battered and beautiful world —

I come before you today not as a politician, not as a philosopher, not as a dreamer, but as a person who can no longer look at the world we have built and pretend it is just. I come before you with a single, urgent proposal, one that will be called radical, that will be called dangerous, that will be called impossible. I call it overdue.

A one-time confiscation of excessive wealth above a fixed, high threshold — to be redistributed for the common good.

Let me say at the outset what I am not proposing. I am not proposing the abolition of private property. I am not proposing the seizure of family homes, small businesses, retirement savings, or the modest comforts earned by a lifetime of honest work. The threshold I speak of would be set extraordinarily high — so high that the vast majority of citizens, even the comfortable, would never feel its edge. I am speaking of fortunes so vast they defy comprehension. Fortunes measured not in lifetimes but in dynasties. Fortunes that, in a single afternoon, could end homelessness in a nation. Fortunes that, hoarded, are a moral obscenity in a world where children go to bed hungry three doors down from where I stand.

The Scale of the Obscenity

Let us speak plainly about what we are tolerating. While you and I have debated, while legislatures have dawdled, while commissions have convened and adjourned — a handful of individuals have accumulated wealth equal to the combined gross domestic product of entire continents. Not earned — extracted. Extracted from labor that was underpaid, from lands that were depleted, from systems that were rigged, from generations that were promised a share and received a pittance.

We do not tax these fortunes adequately. We do not regulate them effectively. We do not, in any meaningful sense, democratically govern them. They govern us. They fund the think tanks that tell us inequality is natural. They fund the campaigns of the politicians who refuse to touch them. They own the media platforms that shape the very vocabulary of our public debate. And we — we the many — are told, again and again, that to challenge this is to be envious, to be ungrateful, to be unrealistic.

I reject this framing utterly.

I am not envious of a man with ten billion dollars. I am appalled. I am appalled that ten billion dollars — a sum no human being could spend in a hundred lifetimes of even the most grotesque extravagance — sits idle, untaxed, hidden, while a single mother works two jobs and chooses between heat and food. I am appalled that the accumulated wealth of one individual could fund universal preschool in a nation, and that it sits instead in offshore accounts, in art vaults, in space programs for the ego of billionaires.

The Moral Argument

There is a word for hoarding essential resources while people suffer and die from their absence. We use this word when one person does it within a family. We use it when a landlord does it to tenants. We have always understood, in our smaller communities, that there is a line beyond which accumulation becomes cruelty.

We have lost that understanding at scale. We have allowed the line to disappear.

The confiscation I propose is not theft. It is restoration. It is the recovery, on behalf of the common wealth, of resources that were never legitimately the private property of any one individual to begin with. No one earns a billion dollars. They extract it, they leverage it, they compound it on the backs of millions of transactions, millions of workers, millions of small acts of public infrastructure, public education, public law and order. The roads their goods travel on were built by our taxes. The educated workers they employ were educated in our schools. The stability they rely upon is maintained by our police and our courts.

A society that permitted this accumulation has a claim on its reversal.

The Practical Argument

But let us set aside, for a moment, the moral case — which to me is conclusive — and speak of the practical.

Extreme inequality is not merely unjust. It is inefficient. It is destabilizing. It is the great sickness of our age, and it produces, with mathematical regularity, the crises we then claim to be shocked by: political extremism, mass migration, the collapse of faith in democratic institutions, the slow suffocation of the middle class, the financial panics that always begin at the top and crash down upon the rest of us.

The redistribution I propose is not punishment. It is vaccination. It is the inoculation of a body politic that is being consumed by a fever. The wealth confiscated would not vanish — it would circulate. It would fund housing, healthcare, education, climate adaptation, debt relief, the infrastructure of a decent life. Money in the hands of the many is not consumed and discarded — it is the very engine of a functioning economy. Every dollar that flows to a family in need flows back into the community, into the shops, into the labor market, into the tax base.

The current system is the radical one. It is radical to permit this. It is radical to defend the indefensible. What I propose is, in fact, the most conservative possible position — a restoration of balance, a return to a world in which no individual holds more than a hundred thousand of their fellow citizens combined.

The Objections, and the Answers

I know what will be said. I know the talking points. I have heard them all my life.

"It will never work." Neither did the abolition of slavery, until it did. Neither did universal suffrage, until it did. History is long, and the impossible is merely the inevitable on a delayed schedule.

"It will discourage innovation." The innovators of this world have never been the billionaires. The innovators are the researchers in universities, the engineers in labs, the workers with ideas — and they are vastly underpaid relative to the value they create. The billionaires are not the risk-takers. They are the owners of the risk-takers. Innovation will not slow. It will accelerate, freed from the distorting influence of hoarded capital.

"It will cause capital flight." Where will it flee to? The world is not a buffet from which the wealthy may pick their jurisdiction. Coordinated international action — a coalition of nations bound by a common moral standard — can close the exits. And the wealthy, stripped of their fortunes once, will learn the meaning of citizenship in a society that has finally stopped tolerating their parasitism.

"It is unjust to take what was legally earned." The law is not morality. The law was written, in large part, by the wealthy and their servants. Laws that permit this accumulation are unjust laws, and the correction of unjust laws is among the highest duties of a free people.

"It sets a dangerous precedent." Yes. It sets the precedent that the common good may, in extremis, override private accumulation. I will defend that precedent to my last breath. It is the precedent of every nation that has ever had the courage to confront its oligarchs.

The Vision

Imagine, for a moment, the morning after.

Imagine a society in which no child is homeless, because the wealth to house them was recovered from those who would never have missed it. Imagine a society in which no family is bankrupted by illness, because the wealth to care for them was restored to the commons. Imagine a society in which every young person, regardless of birth, can climb as far as their gifts will carry them, because the inherited dynasties have been broken. Imagine a society in which a person is valued for what they contribute, not for what they possess. Imagine democracy — real democracy, the kind we have been promised and denied — in which the votes of citizens are not drowned out by the moneyed interests of a few.

This is not a utopia. It is a possibility. It is within our reach, if we have the courage to reach for it.

The Closing

My fellow citizens, I will not pretend this proposal is painless. I will not pretend it is without risk. I will not pretend that the forces arrayed against it are not powerful, entrenched, and accustomed to winning.

But I will say this: every generation is tested. Every generation is asked, in its own hour, whether it will tolerate the intolerable — whether it will accept the world as it is, or whether it will dare to demand the world as it should be.

Our hour is now. The inequality we tolerate is not merely an economic arrangement. It is a moral catastrophe. It is a betrayal of every promise our societies have ever made. And it will not be corrected by appeals to conscience, by polite letters to congressmen, by incremental adjustments at the margins. It will be corrected, if it is corrected at all, by action — by the single, decisive, historic action of a people who have finally had enough.

Let them call it confiscation. I call it justice. Let them call it radical. I call it delayed. Let them call it impossible. I call it inevitable.

The wealth exists. The suffering exists. The choice, my friends, is ours.

Let us choose, at last, to be worthy of the world we could build.

Thank you.

A Bold Step Towards Equity: Why a One-Time Wealth Redistribution is Essential

In an era marked by staggering wealth disparities and growing social unrest, the stark reality of economic inequality has become a defining challenge of our time. While many struggle to afford basic necessities, the world’s billionaires have amassed fortunes exceeding $10,000,000—a threshold that sits incongruously beside the grim statistic that over 700 million people globally face chronic hunger daily. To tackle this disparity and fund vital public programs, a one-time, large-scale confiscation of private wealth holdings above $10 million is a necessary, moral, and economically pragmatic solution. Economic Growth Through Redistribution

Concentrated wealth hoards productive potential. When a small elite controls excessive capital, it often stagnates the economy by reducing broad-based consumer demand and investment in public goods. Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz highlights that rising inequality hampers economic growth by limiting access to education and credit for lower-income groups. A one-time wealth redistribution would inject liquidity into the economy via public spending on infrastructure, research, and social programs, catalyzing job creation and consumer spending—the engines of growth. The $10 million threshold ensures that even ultra-wealthy individuals retain sufficient resources to sustain innovation, as motivations beyond profit—such as legacy-building, societal impact, and innovation—often drive breakthroughs. This targeted approach avoids deterring entrepreneurship while dismantling systemic hoarding practices that drain economic vitality.

Ethical Imperative of Economic Justice

Beyond practical benefits lies a profound moral argument. Philosopher John Rawls’ difference principle posits that inequalities are justified only if they benefit the least advantaged. Today, wealth disparities fail this test; they entrench privilege and perpetuate cycles of poverty. Confiscating wealth above $10 million aligns with utilitarian ethics, maximizing societal welfare by prioritizing basic needs over excess. It is a recognition that resources hoarded in obscene luxury (e.g., private jets, sprawling estates) could instead fund transformative initiatives like universal healthcare and climate resilience, addressing existential threats while uplifting humanity. As Warren Buffett once remarked, “There’s class warfare… and my class is winning,” underscoring the urgency of rebalancing the scales.

Funding Universal Public Programs

The proceeds from such a policy could revolutionize essential sectors. Imagine a world where every child receives quality education, where life-saving vaccines are universally accessible, and where sustainable energy infrastructure is rapidly deployed. These programs, long underfunded due to regressive fiscal policies, would flourish under redirected capital. For instance, investing $3 trillion (a conservative estimate of assets above $10 million in wealthy nations) could fund universal pre-K through college education systems worldwide, erecting a foundation for informed, productive citizens. Similarly, prioritizing renewable energy investments could combat climate change, a crisis disproportionately affecting the global poor. This isn’t fantasy but a logical reallocation to address root causes of inequality and instability.

Critics may decry rights violations or economic collapse, yet these concerns are overblown and solvable. First, the threshold ensures minimal disruption. Over 99.9% of individuals wouldn’t be affected, preserving economic confidence and avoiding capital flight. To safeguard against constitutional challenges, the policy could be framed as an exceptional tax on extreme fortunes, akin to wartime measures, supported by democratic consensus.

Second, the claim that redistribution stifles investment ignores historical precedent. Post-WWII economies thrived under high tax rates on the wealthy, from 1950s America to Scandinavian social democracies. Moreover, confiscation could be paired with policies incentivizing productive investment in the remaining capital, directing it toward socially beneficial ventures.

Third, concerns about governmental inefficiency can be mitigated through transparent, merit-based allocation systems, perhaps anchored by independent oversight boards. Programs like Head Start or the Highway Trust Fund exemplify successful public investments that yield measurable returns, refuting fears of “wasted” funds.

Conclusion: A Patriotic Pursuit of Equity

This proposal isn’t radical—it’s remedial. It is a temporary correction to a system skewed toward the ultra-wealthy, who have long gamed markets and manipulated tax laws to evade contributing their fair share. By taking decisive action, governments can reshape societies into ones where prosperity is shared, not hoarded. The choice is stark: either cling to inequitable systems that breed discord and decay, or embrace a future where collective well-being supersedes individual excess. History’s march toward progress has always hinged on such brave recalibrations. The time to act is now, before inequality further fractures our world. Let us channel the audacity of vision that built nations into a bold step for justice and all humanity’s future.

Introduction

The Moral Case: Wealth Hoarding is Unjust

1. Extreme Wealth is Built on Exploitation

The fortunes of the ultra-rich are not the product of mere hard work or innovation—they are the result of systemic extraction. Billionaires like Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, and Warren Buffett have amassed their wealth through:

  • Labor exploitation (low wages, union-busting, gig economy precarity)
  • Monopolistic practices (corporate consolidation, anti-competitive behavior)
  • Tax avoidance (offshore accounts, loopholes, lobbying for lower rates)
  • Government subsidies (bailouts, infrastructure, R&D funding)

When a single individual holds billions while workers cannot afford rent, that wealth is not "earned"—it is stolen through structural inequality. Confiscating excess wealth is not theft; it is restitution.

2. Wealth Inequality Undermines Democracy

Concentrated wealth translates directly into concentrated power. The richest Americans:

  • Dominate politics through lobbying, dark money, and revolving-door corruption.
  • Control media narratives by owning news outlets and influencing public opinion.
  • Shape policy to benefit their interests (tax cuts, deregulation, austerity).

A functioning democracy cannot coexist with oligarchy. Redistributing extreme wealth is essential to restoring political equality and ensuring that government serves the people, not the plutocrats.

3. Hoarded Wealth Serves No Social Purpose

Beyond a certain point, wealth accumulation becomes purely speculative. A billionaire does not "need" $10 billion—most of it sits in stocks, real estate, or offshore accounts, doing nothing for society. Meanwhile:

  • 40% of Americans cannot cover a $400 emergency.
  • Millions lack healthcare, housing, and food security.
  • Public infrastructure is crumbling.

This wealth could be put to immediate use funding universal healthcare, free college, green energy transitions, and affordable housing. There is no ethical justification for allowing vast fortunes to remain idle while people suffer.

The Economic Case: Confiscation Would Spur Growth and Stability

1. A One-Time Wealth Tax Would Generate Trillions

The ultra-rich hold $45 trillion in wealth—more than the entire U.S. GDP. A one-time confiscation of all wealth above $10 million (affecting roughly 0.1% of households) could raise:

  • $10–15 trillion (conservative estimate)

Unlike incremental tax hikes, a single, sweeping confiscation would provide an immediate fiscal windfall without the political battles of annual budget fights.

Trickle-down economics has failed. When wealth is concentrated at the top, it flows into financial speculation, not productive investment. But when money is in the hands of ordinary people:

  • Consumer spending increases, driving demand and job creation.
  • Small businesses thrive as communities gain purchasing power.
  • Public services improve, reducing long-term costs (e.g., preventive healthcare vs. emergency care).

Historical examples—such as the post-WWII economic boom, fueled by high taxes on the rich and strong social programs—prove that broad-based prosperity drives growth, not billionaire hoarding.

3. It Would Curb Financial Instability

Extreme wealth concentration contributes to asset bubbles, market crashes, and economic fragility. The 2008 financial crisis was exacerbated by deregulated Wall Street elites gambling with public money. A wealth confiscation would:

  • Reduce speculative capital that distorts markets.
  • Decrease systemic risk by breaking up concentrated financial power.
  • Encourage productive investment over extractive finance.

The Political Case: Confiscation is Feasible and Popular

1. Public Support for Wealth Redistribution is Growing

Polls show that majorities of Americans—including many Republicans—support higher taxes on the rich:

  • 72% of voters support a 2% wealth tax on fortunes over $50M (Reuters/Ipsos).
  • 60% believe the wealthy don’t pay their fair share (Pew Research).
  • Younger generations overwhelmingly favor systemic economic reform.

A one-time confiscation, framed as a patriotic reset to fund national renewal, would have broad appeal—especially if paired with tangible benefits like debt relief and universal healthcare.

Critics claim confiscation is "unconstitutional," but history proves otherwise:

  • The U.S. has imposed wealth taxes before (e.g., 94% top marginal rate in the 1940s–50s).
  • Confiscatory policies have been used in crises (e.g., FDR’s gold seizure in 1933, wartime asset seizures).
  • Other nations have implemented wealth taxes (France, Spain, Argentina).

A legally structured confiscation—whether through eminent domain for public good, a one-time surtax, or a wealth cap—could withstand constitutional challenges if designed as a necessary measure for economic survival.

3. The Alternative is Worse: Collapse or Revolution

  • Rising fascism, as disillusioned populations turn to strongmen promising to "drain the swamp."
  • Economic stagnation, as wealth hoarding strangles demand and innovation.

A controlled, democratic redistribution is far preferable to the chaos of collapse or the violence of revolution.

"It’s Theft!"

No—true theft is billionaires paying lower tax rates than nurses while workers subsidize their wealth through austerity. Confiscation is reparations for decades of rigged economic rules.

"The Rich Will Flee!"

"It’s Un-American!"

What’s un-American is dynastic wealth and inherited privilege. The Founding Fathers—including Thomas Paine and Teddy Roosevelt—warned against aristocracy. True patriotism means economic democracy, not oligarchy.

Conclusion: The Time for Half-Measures is Over

Incremental reforms—marginal tax hikes, weak regulations—have failed to reverse inequality. The ultra-rich have too much power, too much wealth, and too little accountability. A one-time confiscation of extreme fortunes is not just justified; it is necessary for survival.

This is not about punishing success—it is about correcting a broken system. No one "earns" a billion dollars in a society where others starve. The choice is clear:

  • Continue down the path of oligarchy, austerity, and collapse, or
  • Reclaim our economy for the many, not the few.

The moment demands boldness. Confiscate the billions. Fund the future. Restore justice. The alternative is unthinkable.

Introduction

We live in an age of grotesque inequality. While millions struggle to afford basic necessities, a tiny elite controls more wealth than the bottom half of humanity. The Moral Imperative

Wealth does not arise in a vacuum. Every fortune is built on a foundation provided by society: public roads and ports, educated workers, legal systems that protect property, and the stability that comes from living in a functioning community. No individual becomes a billionaire solely through personal effort; they rely on the collective labor and infrastructure that we all maintain. Consequently, society has a right to reclaim a portion of that wealth when it grows to obscene levels—especially when so many lack the essentials for a dignified life.

Philosopher John Rawls argued that inequalities are only justified if they benefit the least advantaged members of society. Today’s extreme wealth concentration blatantly violates this principle. The super‑rich hoard resources that could alleviate suffering, improve education, and safeguard our planet. A one‑time confiscation above a generous threshold—$10 million per person—ensures that no one is left destitute; even after the levy, affected individuals will retain enough to live in luxury. The surplus taken is, by definition, superfluous to their well‑being but transformative for the common good.

Moreover, the social contract is not a one‑way street. Those who have benefitted most from the system owe the greatest debt to it. This levy is not punishment; it is a restorative act of justice, rebalancing the scales so that everyone can share in prosperity.

Economic Benefits: A Tide That Lifts All Boats

The economic case for a one‑time wealth confiscation is compelling. Conservative estimates suggest that confiscating all wealth above $10 million in the United States alone would yield tens of trillions of dollars. This colossal injection of capital could eliminate national debt, fully fund universal healthcare, make college tuition‑free, build affordable housing, and finance a Green New Deal to combat climate change. Firstly, these investments would create millions of jobs and stimulate demand across the economy. Unlike tax cuts for the wealthy—which often end up in offshore accounts or speculative assets—money placed in the hands of the middle and lower classes circulates quickly, boosting local businesses and generating further economic activity. Economists agree that increasing the purchasing power of ordinary people is the most effective way to drive sustainable growth.

Secondly, reducing inequality itself spurs economic performance. When people are healthy, educated, and financially secure, they are more productive and innovative. A society with a strong social safety net encourages risk‑taking and entrepreneurship, because failure no longer means destitution. By funding universal programs, we would unlock the full potential of our human capital.

Thirdly, a one‑time levy avoids the distortions associated with permanent high taxes. Because it is not an ongoing drain on wealth accumulation, it minimizes disincentives for future work and investment. After the levy, individuals can again build fortunes up to the threshold, preserving the motivation to innovate and create.

Practicality and Feasibility

Critics often dismiss such a proposal as administratively impossible. Yet modern financial systems are more than capable of executing a one‑time wealth assessment. Governments already track vast amounts of data through tax returns, property registries, and banking records. With the addition of a comprehensive wealth registry—and the political will to enforce it—determining each individual’s net worth above the threshold would be straightforward.

Implementation could follow a clear timeline: declare a valuation date, require all citizens to report their assets and liabilities, and then transfer the surplus (above $10 million) to a public trust fund. To prevent evasion, stringent penalties for non‑compliance and temporary capital controls could be enacted. International cooperation would be necessary to address offshore holdings, but the scale of the levy provides a strong incentive for other nations to participate or risk being seen as tax havens.

History offers ample precedent. After World War II, several European countries imposed one‑time wealth levies to rebuild their shattered economies. In the United States, marginal income tax rates above 90% during the 1950s dramatically reduced inequality without stifling growth. A confiscation above a high threshold is simply a more direct and efficient version of those policies.

Addressing the Objections

Property rights are not absolute; they are creations of society and can be limited when the public good demands it. Eminent domain, zoning laws, and progressive taxation are everyday examples. A one‑time wealth confiscation is a legitimate exercise of democratic power to rectify an existential crisis of inequality. The Moral and Economic Imperative of a One-Time Wealth Confiscation to Fund Public Good

Introduction

The concentration of wealth in the hands of a tiny fraction of the population has reached unprecedented levels, creating a society where extreme inequality undermines democracy, stifles economic mobility, and perpetuates systemic injustice. The case for such a measure is built on moral, economic, and political grounds, making it a necessary step toward a fairer and more functional society.

I. The Moral Case: Wealth Hoarding is a Form of Theft from Society

A. The Ultra-Rich Did Not Earn Their Wealth Through Merit Alone

The myth of the "self-made billionaire" is a dangerous fiction. Wealth accumulation above $10 million is almost never the result of individual effort alone—it is the product of systemic advantages, including:

  • Inherited wealth – The vast majority of ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs) inherit significant portions of their fortunes. According to the Institute for Policy Studies, the wealthiest 0.1% of Americans control $30 trillion, much of which was passed down through generations.

  • State-subsidized infrastructure and education – Billionaires benefit from publicly funded roads, universities, and research institutions that they did not pay for. Without these, their wealth would not exist.
  • Monopoly power and rent-seeking – Many fortunes are built on artificial scarcity, lobbying, and market manipulation rather than innovation. Jeff Bezos, for example, did not "invent" e-commerce—he dominated it by crushing competitors and using predatory pricing.

If wealth above $10 million is not earned through pure merit but through systemic privilege, then hoarding it is not just unfair—it is a form of theft from society.

B. Extreme Wealth Undermines Social Trust and Democracy

A society where a handful of people control more wealth than entire nations is inherently unstable. The top 1% owns 40% of all U.S. wealth, while the bottom 50% owns just 2.6%. This concentration of power:

  • Distorts political representation – The ultra-rich buy influence through lobbying, campaign donations, and media control. The Citizens United decision allowed corporations to spend unlimited money on elections, ensuring that policy favors the wealthy.
  • Erodes social cohesion – When people see billionaires avoiding taxes while teachers and nurses struggle, public trust in institutions collapses. The 2020 protests against police brutality were fueled by decades of economic neglect—a direct result of wealth hoarding.
  • Justifies authoritarianism – History shows that extreme inequality leads to fascism or revolution. The Occupy Wall Street movement was a warning: when people feel exploited, they will demand radical change—whether through violent uprising or democratic reform.

A one-time confiscation would restore balance by ensuring that wealth serves the many, not the few.

  • Wage stagnation persists – When CEOs make 300x more than workers, productivity gains go to the top. Wealth confiscation would force a rebalancing, raising wages and reducing exploitation.

The 2008 financial crisis was partly caused by wealth concentration—banks had too much power, leading to reckless lending. A one-time confiscation would break up monopolies, prevent too-big-to-fail institutions, and ensure that financial power is democratized.

A. The Ultra-Rich Have Captured the Political System

The problem is not lack of public support—it’s lack of political will. The ultra-rich control the media, the courts, and the legislative process, making incremental reforms impossible. A one-time confiscation would be a nuclear option—but sometimes, nuclear options are necessary to break deadlocks.

The real question is not whether it’s possible—but whether we have the courage to do it.

Rebuttal: The ultra-rich do not invest their wealth productively—they hoard it in tax shelters, real estate, and financial assets that do not create jobs. Studies show that redistribution actually boosts growth by increasing consumer demand.

The concentration of wealth in the hands of a few is not an economic law—it is a political choice. The ultra-rich have rigged the system to ensure that their fortunes grow while the rest of society suffers. Incremental reforms—like higher marginal tax rates or closing loopholes—will not work because the rich will lobby, litigate, and lobby some more until they are weakened.

A one-time, large-scale confiscation of wealth above $10 million is not just fair—it is necessary to:

  1. Fund essential public programs (healthcare, education, green energy).
  2. Break the political power of the ultra-rich.
  3. Restore economic democracy where wealth serves the many, not the few.

This is not about punishing success—it’s about correcting a system that has been rigged against the majority for decades. The question is no longer whether we can afford this—but whether we can afford not to.

The time for half-measures is over. The time for radical justice is now.

Extreme wealth concentration enables a small group of individuals to wield disproportionate influence over the political process, leading to policies that favor the wealthy and further exacerbate inequality. To minimize disruption and ensure fairness, the confiscation should be conducted in a transparent and gradual manner. A clear and reasonable threshold should be set, and exemptions could be made for businesses and assets that create jobs and benefit the wider economy. The confiscated wealth should be managed by an independent body tasked with reinvesting it into public programs and ensuring accountability.

Conclusion

In conclusion, a one-time, large-scale state confiscation of private wealth holdings above a fixed high threshold is a necessary measure to fund essential public programs, reduce inequality, promote economic growth, and prevent oligarchy. While it may be a contentious policy, it offers a swift and effective solution to pressing societal challenges.
